desc:
You maintain a multiset of integers that starts empty. The array ops lists operations, each given as [type, x]:

  • [1, x]: insert the value x (duplicates are allowed).
  • [2, x]: remove one copy of the value x. It is guaranteed that a copy exists.
  • [3, k]: query the k-th smallest element of the multiset (counting duplicates, k = 1 is the minimum). It is guaranteed that 1 ≤ k ≤ size.

Return the answers to the type-3 operations, in order.

ops = [[1,5],[1,2],[1,9],[3,2],[2,2],[3,2],[1,5],[3,2]]
set {2,5,9}      -> 2nd smallest 5
remove 2: {5,9}  -> 2nd smallest 9
insert 5: {5,5,9} -> 2nd smallest 5
answer = [5, 9, 5]
constraints: type is 1, 2 or 3; every operation is valid as described
hints: Keeping a sorted list and using binary search to find insert and delete positions is the simplest start. What does each update cost in the worst case?
All inserted values are known in advance, so they can be compressed to ranks 1..m. Then the multiset is just an array of counts over ranks.
A Fenwick tree over the counts supports add and remove in O(log m), and a binary-lifting descent on the tree finds the k-th element in O(log m).
editorial: Read all operations first and compress the set of inserted values to ranks. Maintain a Fenwick (binary indexed) tree where position r holds how many copies of the r-th smallest value are present. Insert and removal are point updates of +1 and -1.

To answer a query for the k-th smallest, descend the Fenwick tree from the highest power of two: at each step try to jump step positions ahead; if the count stored there is still less than k, take the jump and subtract that count from k. When no jump is possible, the next position is the rank of the answer.

Every operation is O(log m), giving O(q log q) in total. Inserting into a plain Python sorted list is also accepted for small inputs (O(n) per update through memmove), but the Fenwick descent scales to millions of operations.
